name: Philemon
description: Household assembly · affection · debt · partnership · reception as a brother

1.text: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, our beloved fellow worker,
to the beloved Apphia, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the assembly in your house:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I thank my God always, making mention of you in my prayers,
hearing of your love and of the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints,
that the fellowship of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus.
For we have much joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.
Therefore though I have all boldness in Christ to command you that which is appropriate,
yet for love’s sake I rather appeal to you, being such a one as Paul, the aged, but also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.
I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whom I have become the father of in my chains,
who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me.
I am sending him back. Therefore receive him, that is, my own heart,
whom I desired to keep with me, that on your behalf he might serve me in my chains for the Good News.
But I was willing to do nothing without your consent, that your goodness would not be as of necessity, but of free will.
For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever,
no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.
But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account.
I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides).
Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord.
Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say.
Also, prepare a guest room for me, for I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.
Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you,
as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

chapters.title: Receiving Onesimus as a brother tests love within an unequal relationship
chapters.summary: Paul, a prisoner, writes with Timothy to Philemon and the assembly in his house. Paul thanks God for Philemon’s love and faith. He could command, but he appeals out of love. He appeals for Onesimus, who became his child during his imprisonment. Paul sends him back and calls him his own heart. He asks Philemon to receive him as a beloved brother, more than a slave. Paul will repay anything Onesimus owes. He asks for a guest room and sends greetings.
chapters.meaning: Verse 8 says Paul could command Philemon and chooses to appeal. Verse 16 asks that Onesimus be received as a beloved brother. Verse 17 puts the request in terms of partnership. If Philemon counts Paul a partner, he must receive Onesimus as he would Paul. That puts the returning servant in the apostle’s place at the door. Verse 18 removes the money objection: Paul will pay what is owed. Verse 21 adds that Paul expects Philemon to do even more than he asks.

lds.text: Why does receiving Onesimus as Paul himself make partnership costly?

chapters.historicalNote: The household assembly shares the greeting, so the appeal reaches beyond a private exchange. Praise for Philemon's love prepares the request that he receive Onesimus as Paul's own heart. Paul chooses an appeal over a command, yet remembered obligation gives that appeal real pressure. His offer to carry any debt makes partnership costly rather than merely a friendly title. Pietz emphasizes changed relationships while recognizing that the letter does not clearly require legal freedom. The promised visit leaves Philemon facing continued accountability, while Onesimus's own response remains unrecorded.
chapters.mapNote: The letter names no place, so the map shows no point.
chapters.routeEvidence: The letter gives no travel route.

people.name: Paul
people.role: Prisoner who writes to Philemon about Onesimus
people.relations: He names Timothy beside himself and asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a partner.
people.meaning: Paul writes from chains and calls himself aged. He chooses to appeal and not to command. He asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul. He offers to repay anything Onesimus owes, and he signs this with his own hand.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: Brother named with Paul in the greeting
people.relations: Paul calls him a brother before addressing the household assembly.
people.meaning: Paul names Timothy as a brother in the first line. Timothy sends the greeting with Paul. The letter says nothing else about him.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Jesus Christ
people.role: Lord named in the greetings, the thanks, and the blessing
people.relations: Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus. He ends with grace from the Lord Jesus Christ.
people.meaning: Paul gives thanks for Philemon’s faith toward the Lord Jesus. He asks that Onesimus be a beloved brother in the Lord. The letter ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Philemon
people.role: Beloved fellow worker asked to receive Onesimus
people.relations: Paul praises his love and asks him to receive Onesimus as Paul himself.
people.meaning: Paul thanks Philemon for his love and for refreshing the saints. Then Paul asks him to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother. Paul wants Philemon to act by free will. Paul also asks him to prepare a guest room.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Onesimus
people.role: Paul’s child, sent back to Philemon
people.relations: Paul calls him his child and own heart, and offers to carry any debt.
people.meaning: Paul became his father in chains. Paul calls him once useless and now useful. Paul sends him back to Philemon and asks Philemon to receive him as a brother. The letter does not say how Philemon answered.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Epaphras
people.relations: Paul names him before Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke.
people.meaning: Paul calls Epaphras his fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus. Epaphras sends greetings to Philemon. The letter says nothing else about him.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.
